NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday directed the appellate tribunals hearing appeals related to the West Bengal Special Intensive Revision (SIR) to give preference to pleas filed by voters challenging their exclusion from the electoral rolls, while deferring those contesting the inclusion of names.A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked the tribunals to separate appeals challenging voter exclusions from those contesting inclusions, and give priority to the exclusions."The second set of appeals (inclusion) does not involve any urgency, and those appeals may, for the time being, be deferred. The first set of appeals (exclusions) shall be given preference in the matter of final disposal," the bench said in its order, LiveLaw reported.The bench further directed the tribunals to prioritise, within the exclusion-related appeals, cases involving voters under the jurisdiction of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation, given that civic body elections are due to be held soon.The Supreme Court also directed the Election Commission (EC) to increase the number of appellate tribunals hearing appeals related to the West Bengal SIR, in consultation with the chief justice of the Calcutta high court.The top court was hearing petitions seeking steps to streamline and expedite the disposal of appeals before the tribunals set up to address grievances arising from SIR in the state.On August 25, the bench had directed the EC to submit details of pending and disposed-of appeals, with a separate count of cases filed by voters challenging their exclusion from or inclusion in the electoral rolls.The court had also asked the poll panel to specify how many additional tribunals would be needed to ensure that the appeals were decided within a stipulated timeframe.
Article Summary: The Supreme Court on Monday directed the appellate tribunals hearing appeals related to the West Bengal Special Intensive Revision (SIR) to give preference to pleas filed by voters challenging their exclusion from the electoral rolls. A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said the second set of appeals (inclusion) does not involve any urgency, and those appeals may, for the time being, be deferred.

Article Title: 'Disappearing Faces': Tamannaah Bhatia, Vishal Bhardwaj discuss Sadhguru's photo book on Himalayan communities
Article Text:
Sadhguru, Tamannaah Bhatia discuss ageing, individuality and education at Mumbai event

Discussion on individuality and education

About 'Disappearing Faces'

Actor Tamannaah Bhatia and filmmaker Vishal Bhardwaj joined spiritual leader Sadhguru for a discussion on his photo book Disappearing Faces at the Fairmont Hotel in Mumbai on November 22.The conversation covered ageing, individuality, education, devotion and the changing lifestyles of people living in remote Himalayan regions.The book brings together photographs taken by Sadhguru over five decades of journeys through the Himalayas, particularly Nepal and Tibet. The portraits document people and communities whose lives have been shaped by their relationship with the natural environment.During the discussion, Tamannaah spoke about the photographs' portrayal of ageing and contrasted the acceptance of visible signs of ageing among the people captured in the book with attitudes in urban society.“Why are we not accepting of something that's the most inevitable, which is the passage of time?” she asked, observing that the people in the photographs appeared more accepting of ageing than those living in cities.Responding to her remarks, Sadhguru said attitudes towards ageing in India had changed in recent times. “This is, I think, a recent happening in India. Otherwise, women and men grew old gracefully in this country.But we have taken Western ideas where the whole civilizations are ruled by hormones,” he said.He added that society had come to place excessive importance on youth and the age associated with peak hormonal activity. “But if you make one aspect of life everything, then you will be a very skewed life,” he said.The conversation also examined the individuality of the people featured in the photographs. Tamannaah noted that despite having fewer resources, education and exposure than their urban counterparts, the people appeared to have distinct personalities and a greater sense of comfort in expressing themselves.Sadhguru linked this to the purpose of education, arguing that it was increasingly focused on preparing people for employment rather than encouraging them to explore their interests and capabilities.“Education should be about expanding our horizons,” he said, adding that many people remained occupied with securing jobs, leaving limited room to explore what they were capable of or inclined towards.Bhardwaj, meanwhile, drew attention to the stillness visible in the faces captured in the book. He referred to Sadhguru's observation that stillness represented the highest level of intensity and asked how this related to the devotional lives of saints such as Meera and Kabir.Sadhguru explained that Meera's devotion to Krishna shaped her emotional experiences, allowing her to approach everything with a sense of sweetness. Kabir, he said, sought to balance his inner experiences with the practical demands of everyday life.He also referred to Krishna as an example of being fully engaged with the world without allowing external circumstances to disturb one's inner experience.Launched in August, Disappearing Faces is a collection of photographs taken by Sadhguru during his journeys through remote Himalayan regions over five decades.The book focuses particularly on communities in Nepal and Tibet, documenting their faces, lifestyles and experiences.According to the book's description, the photographs capture ways of life that are changing with the spread of modern development and the influence of the information age.
Article Summary: Actor Tamannaah Bhatia and filmmaker Vishal Bhardwaj joined spiritual leader Sadhguru for a discussion on his photo book Disappearing Faces at the Fairmont Hotel in Mumbai on November 22. The conversation covered ageing, individuality, education, devotion and the changing lifestyles of people living in remote Himalayan regions.

NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath penned an emotional letter to his late mother, Savitri Devi , recalling a deeply personal moment from his life as a monk when he returned home in saffron robes to seek alms from her. The letter, published in the latest edition of ‘Mukhyamantri Pati’, comes days after his 91-year-old mother passed away at her native village in Uttarakhand.Savitri Devi died on Friday morning at her ancestral home in Panchur village in Pauri Garhwal district. Her mortal remains were taken to Namami Gange Ghat, also known as Chandi Ghat, in Haridwar on Saturday for the last rites. Adityanath gave a shoulder to his mother's mortal remains and was seen getting emotional as he paid his final respects.Following her death, the chief minister shared a tribute on X, writing: “There is no shade like a mother’s, no refuge like a mother’s. There is no protection like a mother’s, no love like a mother’s.”In his latest letter, written in Hindi and titled ‘Yogi Ki Pati’, Adityanath dedicated his message to mothers and wrote: “This letter is dedicated to every mother, without whom life would not exist. Without mothers, neither you nor I would be here. No living being would have an existence, and this world itself would not exist. A mother is not merely the one who gives birth; she is the mother of the universe.Even God has a mother. ”“Today, once again, my eyes fill with tears as I remember every mother,” Yogi wrote, recalling the blessings of Mata Kaushalya when Lord Ram left for exile and Lord Krishna's journey from the prison in Mathura to Gokul at his mother's wish. “A mother can take the place of anyone, but no one can ever take the place of a mother. A mother's affection is the most beautiful emotion in the world.”The chief minister also recounted an incident from more than three years after he embraced monastic life. Standing outside his home in Panchur in saffron robes, he called out to his mother for alms, as required by the monastic tradition.“Mother, please give me alms,” he recalled saying. His mother, struggling to understand the sight before her, asked: “Son, what have you done to yourself? Is there nothing to eat at home that you have to beg for alms?”Adityanath said he replied: “Mother, renunciation is my duty. A yogi’s hunger can only be satisfied through alms. Mother, I have not come to stay here; I have come to seek alms. Whatever you offer will fulfil my purpose.”In a post on X accompanying the message, Adityanath said the values of Sanatan Dharma were rooted in reverence for mothers. “Some debts can never be repaid. Yes, we can certainly fulfil our duty. Since entering public life, I have been striving to fulfil this duty towards the mothers of our state,” he wrote.“The true mark of respect for every mother would be for every resident of the state to take a pledge today: to become a source of support for a mother without anyone to care for her, to understand the pain of a deprived mother, and to bring a smile to the face of a mother in distress.”The post's accompanying photograph also carried a link to the Uttar Pradesh government's Women and Child Development Department website.
Article Summary: Yogi Adityanath penned an emotional letter to his late mother, Savitri Devi, recalling a deeply personal moment from his life as a monk. The letter, published in the latest edition of ‘Mukhyamantri Pati’, comes days after his 91-year-old mother passed away.

Article Title: NHAI puts 50,000 km of highways under dashcam watch, to automate penalties for contractors
Article Text:
NHAI has rolled out a system for weekly monitoring of 40 types of defects

Dashcams detecting highway defects

NEW DELHI: Highway concessionaires, maintenance contractors and NHAI officials will no longer be able to dodge or delay action on defects, such as potholes, faded road markings, rutting and faulty lights, which remain major recurring problems on NH stretches.NHAI has rolled out a system for weekly monitoring of 40 types of defects through dashcams installed in patrolling vehicles covering nearly 50,000 km of NH network.NHAI officials said that not only will data and details be collected with exact location and visual evidence, but these will also be shared with respective contractors responsible for specific stretches.“The dashcams can detect potholes as small as two inches pothole. Currently, failing to rectify defect within a set timeline attracts penalties, which are calculated as per contract conditions. In the next couple of months, the penalty calculation will become automatic. We have been sensitising contractors and officers for the past two months,” said a senior NHAI official.This covers all NH stretches under NHAI that are under operation and maintenance. This is significant considering that the highways authority has faced public ire over poor maintenance of several road stretches.Data accessed by TOI showed that 92,088 defects were detected through dashcam recordings since the exercise was rolled out two months back. Nearly 23% of these related to faded road markings and around 15% to potholes. While nearly 72% of the defects were rectified, around 17% remain overdue for rectification.As per the set timelines, contractors get two days to fill potholes, one day to fix defunct lights and safety issues at work zones, and seven days to close unauthorised openings, to name a few.“Since the details of defects are backed by evidence and every contractor and field officer can see them on our central server, there is no question of any dispute. Highway contractors also understand that timely maintenance reduces their burden. The defects are closed only when details of rectification with pictorial evidence are uploaded and verified,” said another NHAI official.TOI has learnt that at a later stage, the public would also be able see the details and give their feedback.
Article Summary: NHAI has rolled out a system for weekly monitoring of 40 types of defects through dashcams installed in patrolling vehicles covering nearly 50,000 km of NH network. Data and details will also be shared with respective contractors responsible for specific stretches. This is significant considering that the highways authority has faced public ire over poor maintenance of several road stretches.

NEW DELHI: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India ( FSSAI ) has sanctioned prosecution against five food businesses, including Bisleri International Pvt Ltd, over food products found unsafe or substandard, while suspending the licences of two other establishments over serious food safety and hygiene violations.FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri over a sample of packaged drinking water that was found non-compliant with prescribed bromate limits and declared unsafe under Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The Referral Food Laboratory too declared it unsafe after detecting polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. Bisleri International was contacted for its response but had not responded till the time this report was filed.Vasant Masala Pvt Ltd was prosecuted after its chilli powder was found to contain difenoconazole, a pesticide residue, above the allowed limit. Tit-Bit Foods (India) Pvt Ltd faced prosecution over its pre-packed chilli powder containing excess pesticide residues and turmeric powder containing tin above the permitted limit.Mimansa Industries Private Limited faced prosecution over walnut kernels found substandard and unsafe. Asha Confectionery faced prosecution over chocolate-filled cookies found misbranded, substandard and unsafe due to discrepancies in declared sugar values.FSSAI has also suspended licences of Urmi Lifesciences LLP and Gaur Ayurvedic Store over poor hygiene and repacking issues respectively.

Article Title: Help just a call away? How emergency system responds in race against time
Article Text:
What happens after that call is made?

Ambulance Services in India – Are the Sirens Loud Enough!

Ambulance delays

Why every minute matters

Health Emergency system

The first response: What should you do when an emergency strikes?

Recent cases: When ambulance delays put lives at risk

The gap in calling and receiving the help

Are India's ambulances and emergency services adequately equipped?

Are emergency helplines working when people need them most?

Ambulance availability

Covid exposed the gaps: What India has learnt?

What needs to change

“Repeated calls went unanswered,” recalls Kishan, describing his family's experience during a medical emergency involving his parents.A medical emergency rarely comes with a warning. A sudden cardiac arrest, a road accident or a stroke can turn an ordinary day into a race against time, where every passing minute can mean the difference between life and death. In such moments, one call for help is often the first and most critical step.But what happens after that call is made?From the moment someone dials 108 or 112 to the ambulance reaching the patient and transporting them to a hospital, multiple layers of emergency response are expected to work seamlessly. The call must be answered, an ambulance dispatched, first responders equipped to handle the crisis and hospitals prepared to provide immediate treatment.Yet, delays at any stage can cost a patient their chance of survival.The 2022 review articleby Sonali Randhawa and Sunil Nandraj estimates that approximately 24,012 people die every day in India due to delays in receiving timely medical assistance.The term 'golden hour' is often used in emergency medicine to describe the importance of getting patients appropriate treatment quickly.But the urgency can be even greater in some conditions.“In a cardiac arrest, the chance of survival falls steeply with every minute that passes without CPR,” says Dr Rajiv Jain, HOD and consultant – Emergency Medicine, Gleneagles BGS Hospital. In a heart attack, delays can cause further damage to the heart muscle, while a stroke requires timely treatment to reduce the risk of lasting brain injury.He adds that in trauma cases, studies suggest only about 20% of accident victims reach medical care within the golden hour. Delays can affect not just survival but also the extent of disability a patient may face.Calling an ambulance early is important because trained crews can begin treatment during the journey and alert the hospital before arrival.Knowing what to do while waiting for professional help can make a crucial difference.Dr Jain says the first step is to stay calm, call emergency services and clearly communicate the location and nature of the emergency. The caller should put the phone on speaker so that the operator can guide them.“If they aren't, start chest compressions at once. Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest, at about 100 to 120 compressions a minute, and keep going until help arrives or the person starts to respond,” he says, referring to a person who is unresponsive and not breathing normally.For heavy bleeding, firm pressure should be applied to the wound. An accident victim should not be moved unnecessarily, particularly if a spinal injury is suspected. Food or water should never be given to an unconscious person.“Those first five minutes belong to the bystander, and they often decide the outcome,” Dr Jain says.But what happens if help arrives late?India has expanded its emergency ambulance network, but how effectively does it function when lives are on the line? Recent incidents from across the country have once again raised questions about the reliability of emergency transport.In Madhya Pradesh's Mandla, a young man struggling to breathe died after a government ambulance allegedly ran out of oxygen.In Kalyan, a 70-year-old man with chest pain died outside a railway station, with his family alleging that the 108 ambulance took around 40 minutes to arrive.In Odisha, the family of a critically ill man alleged that the ambulance transporting him from Cuttack to a private facility in Bhubaneswar stopped on a bridge because it had run out of fuel.While the circumstances differ, these incidents point to a common concern: a delay or failure at any stage of emergency transport can put an already vulnerable patient at greater risk.According to Dr Jain, delays are often caused by a combination of factors: traffic, difficulty locating the patient, lack of advance communication with the hospital, registration queues and waiting for a specialist.“The right hospital matters as much as the nearest one,” he says, adding that sending a patient to a facility without the required treatment can lead to further delays.Dr Anshul Kumar Jain, Director – Cardiology, CK Birla Hospital, Delhi, also stresses the importance of choosing a hospital that can provide immediate stabilisation and life-saving treatment. It may not always be necessary to travel to a bigger hospital if an appropriately equipped facility is closer.India has multiple emergency numbers, including 108 and 112. The latter brings police, fire and ambulance services under one platform. However, the time taken by a first responder to reach a location should not be confused with the time taken by a medically equipped ambulance to arrive.The 2022 review article also mentions that the recommended ambulance-to-population ratio is one road ambulance for every 1 lakh people in the plains and one for every 70,000 people in hilly and tribal areas.However, assessing India's actual ambulance availability remains difficult, as government data from different sources appears inconsistent. The availability of ambulances also does not automatically mean that patients will receive the required level of care.The review cites a 2018 assessment by Centralised Accident and Trauma Services (CATS) Delhi, which found that out of 265 state-run ambulances, only 31 had advanced life support facilities such as defibrillators and ventilators. Around 60 were non-operational due to mechanical faults, while nearly 155 were more than six years old.Dr Rajiv Jain says India's ambulance coverage may appear close to international benchmarks on paper, but vehicles are unevenly distributed and many are basic life support ambulances rather than advanced life support vehicles.During the second wave of Covid-19 in 2021, the demand for private ambulances in Delhi increased fivefold compared with previous months, amid a shortage of adequately equipped public ambulances. Private ambulance operators also charged higher rates, according to the review.The gap between having an emergency helpline and getting timely assistance is also reflected in Delhi's ambulance services.A CAG audit recorded 49 instances in February 2020 when CATS ambulances refused emergency calls. Reasons included a lack of staff, unavailability of oxygen and vehicles being unfit to drive.The Delhi government's 2024-25 annual report, meanwhile, recorded an average CATS ambulance response time of 16.91 minutes.The growing use of app-based ambulance services has also brought the issue into focus. Blinkit ambulances have featured in accounts of people turning to private platforms when conventional options appeared slow or unavailable.In one instance reported in November 2026, a Delhi man said he opted for a Blinkit ambulance after waiting for a response to his call to 112 during his grandmother's medical emergency. The ambulance reportedly reached his home in eight minutes.In another case, a woman said her family struggled to arrange a cab during an early-morning emergency involving her aunt, who had suffered a seizure. They eventually booked a free ambulance through Blinkit.The Covid-19 pandemic exposed how quickly emergency healthcare systems can become overwhelmed when demand rises sharply. Ambulances, hospital beds and oxygen became difficult to access, while families struggled to identify facilities that could admit patients.“Covid showed that our system was built for routine demand, not for a surge. Oxygen, beds and ambulances all became scarce at the same time,” says Dr Rajiv Jain.Dr Anshul Kumar Jain says the pandemic showed that emergency healthcare cannot function as a collection of independent hospitals and ambulance providers. It needs to operate as a coordinated network, where ambulance crews can identify which hospital has the required facilities and capacity before transporting a patient.Recalling her family's experience during the Covid-19 pandemic, Kishan, a Delhi resident, said arranging an ambulance during a medical emergency was a major challenge.“Repeated calls went unanswered as the lines remained busy, putting the patient's life at risk.”“It is the responsibility of the authorities to ensure that emergency helpline numbers remain functional and accessible to everyone, especially during a crisis. It is their failure when they cannot provide even basic facilities inside an ambulance. There was no bed inside the ambulance. We keep coming across reports of patients losing their lives because essential facilities are not made available in time. These delays can prove fatal,” he said.For Dr Jain, improving emergency response requires more than adding ambulances.The system needs quicker dispatch, trained crews, advance alerts to hospitals, real-time information on facilities and clear accountability when delays occur.“What we need now is accountability: published response times, GPS-tagged ambulances, hospital capability grading, trauma registries, and a review of every preventable death as a system failure, not just bad luck,” he says. “When a life is lost in transit, the question must be what failed, not who was unlucky.”Dr Harshitha Sridhar, HOD and Consultant – Emergency Medicine, Manipal Hospital Millers Road, says strengthening the culture of first responders is equally important.“We also need to strengthen the culture of first responders. Police personnel, traffic police, security guards, teachers, public transport staff and even ordinary citizens should receive basic CPR and first-aid training.“India needs to move from a predominantly ambulance-transport model to a prehospital emergency medical care model. An effective emergency response system must be capable of saving lives before a patient reaches the hospital.”For Kishan, who lost a family member, the experience remains a reminder of how helpless families can feel when every minute matters.He suggests people to keep emergency contacts handy and ensure that family members are prepared to act quickly.“Family members should also know how to drive, preferably more than one person. During an emergency, we cannot always depend on ambulances to arrive on time,” he says.An emergency call should bring assistance, not leave them waiting and wondering if help will arrive in time.
Article Summary: India has expanded its emergency ambulance network, but how effectively does it function when lives are on the line? Recent incidents from across the country have once again raised questions about the reliability of emergency transport. Approximately 24,012 people die every day in India due to delays in receiving timely medical assistance.

Article Title: Half a course, full consequences: How India is losing its antibiotics
Article Text:
How India is losing its antibiotics

A problem that has moved into the clinic

What hospital laboratories are finding

Why

antibiotics

are prescribed when they may not be needed

The half-finished course

When the first drug fails

What the rules say

What the government is attempting

A caution about the numbers

What one doctor would change

Most Indian households know the routine. A fever lingers, a half-used strip of tablets from an earlier illness sits in the drawer, and the corner chemist asks few questions. Two doses later the fever eases and the strip goes back into the drawer. It feels like a small, sensible saving.Inside the body, the picture is different. The bacteria that survive a partial course are often the hardiest ones, and they are left free to multiply. Multiplied across millions of households, hospitals, pharmacies and farms, this is how a medicine stops working.Antimicrobial resistance occurs when bacteria develop the ability to survive medicines that once killed them. An infection that a common antibiotic could treat becomes harder to control, pushing doctors toward stronger, costlier drugs.Doctors say they see this daily. Dr Sowmya Muralikumaran, an internal medicine specialist at Apollo Spectra hospital in Chennai, is asked how often she now sees infections that do not respond to the first antibiotic prescribed."Very often," she says, "especially with patients who have self-medicated with multiple medicines before coming for a consultation."The national picture is documented in the annual report of the Indian Council of Medical Research's (ICMR) Antimicrobial Resistance Research and Surveillance Network, which for 2025 analysed 1,13,008 culture-positive bacterial and fungal samples from 30 tertiary-care hospitals. For the first time, it also included data from 34 secondary-care hospitals, 12 of them district hospitals, which contributed another 20,529 samples.The findings are stark. Only 18.4 per cent of E. coli samples responded to cefotaxime and 24.7 per cent to ceftazidime. Among E. coli from urine samples, just 9 per cent were sensitive to ciprofloxacin and 18.2 per cent to levofloxacin. Low sensitivity was seen even among patients visiting outpatient departments, which suggests resistance is not confined to those admitted to hospital.Klebsiella pneumoniae, which can cause bloodstream and lung infections, fared worse. Sensitivity to third-generation cephalosporins was between 23 and 27 per cent. Carbapenems, powerful drugs that doctors turn to when others fail, worked against only 35 to 40 per cent of samples. The report found genes such as OXA-48 and NDM, which help bacteria survive carbapenems, in some Klebsiella samples.Intensive care units showed the heaviest burden. Sensitivity of ICU Klebsiella samples to ertapenem, imipenem and meropenem was 26.1, 24.9 and 26.3 per cent, respectively. Among Acinetobacter baumannii samples that were retested, 91.1 per cent were resistant to carbapenems. More than half of Staphylococcus aureus samples (56.8 per cent) from tertiary hospitals were methicillin-resistant, or MRSA, and about one in five enterococci samples was resistant to vancomycin.Typhoid shows how uneven the picture can be. Samples remained highly sensitive to azithromycin (99.4 per cent) and ceftriaxone (96.6 per cent), but only 2 per cent responded to ciprofloxacin.There is some good news. Fosfomycin worked against 96.5 per cent of urine E. coli samples and nitrofurantoin against 79.1 per cent. The report is clear that these are laboratory findings, and the right drug still depends on the site and severity of infection and on the patient's own tests.Doctors do not always prescribe antibiotics because patients demand them, but expectations play a part. Dr Muralikumaran points to two reasons."Many people have this feeling that only when they take antibiotics will they heal," she says. The second reason lies with the doctor. "There is uncertainty in diagnosis. Mostly all of us might have a viral infection, but sometimes it might be bacterial, so in fear of missing a bacterial infection, an antibiotic can be prescribed too."Antibiotics do not act on viruses. Yet a viral and a bacterial illness can look alike in the first days, and without a quick, affordable test the cautious choice is often to prescribe.The patient's side of the story begins before the consultation. "Quite many have already taken antibiotics," Dr Muralikumaran says. "What they usually do is, after one or two doses, they will feel fine and drop it. They will not fully finish their course."Self-medication then complicates what comes next. A patient who arrives after taking several medicines at home presents a doctor with a muddier clinical picture and, possibly, a more resistant infection.Once an antibiotic fails, she says, swapping it for another is not enough. "Simply recommending an antibiotic will not help." The patient has to be reassessed: symptoms re-examined, more detailed blood tests ordered, and only then a higher antibiotic prescribed, sometimes by a different route.The ICMR report makes a similar point. It highlights that identifying the specific resistance mechanism can help doctors decide which newer medicines may work, and it advises choosing antibiotics based on laboratory testing rather than on what worked in the past.The cost falls on the patient. "It does have a cost on their finances," Dr Muralikumaran says, "and their recovery time also might get delayed."On paper, India restricts how antibiotics are sold. They are listed under Schedules H and H1 of the Drugs Rules, 1945, which means a registered medical practitioner's prescription is needed. Schedule H1, in force since 2014, adds stricter conditions: pharmacies must record each sale in a separate register, and under the rules, these supply records are to be kept for three years.The health ministry's Red Line campaign asks the public not to use medicines marked with a red vertical line, including antibiotics, without a doctor's prescription.Enforcement is another matter. Studies of retail practice have found that over-the-counter sale of antibiotics remains widespread despite these measures. A 2019 study in Kerala that interviewed pharmacy owners found a general perception that the regulations were poorly enforced, and that awareness of the Red Line campaign was patchy, even among healthcare professionals.India's policy effort stretches back more than a decade. The country formed a National Task Force on AMR Containment in 2010 and published its first National Action Plan on AMR in 2017. The second, NAP-AMR 2.0 for 2025 to 2029, was launched by Union Health Minister J P Nadda on 18 November 2025, the first day of the World Health Organization's World AMR Awareness Week.At the launch, Nadda said the misuse and overuse of antibiotics had become an unfortunate common practice. The health ministry said the new plan addresses gaps in the first by increasing ownership of AMR efforts, improving coordination between sectors and engaging more closely with the private sector. It follows a One Health approach, which treats human, animal and environmental health together.Some states have moved on their own. Kerala was the first state to introduce a state action plan on AMR, in 2018. In January 2024, its Drug Control Department launched Operation AMRITH, which involves surprise inspections of pharmacies to detect sales of antibiotics without a prescription. Pharmacies must display a notice saying antibiotics will not be sold without one and must keep accurate sales records. Citizens can report violations on a toll-free number.The ICMR figures come from hospital laboratories, largely tertiary-care centres, and they show how many samples responded to a drug in testing. They do not show how many patients failed treatment, developed complications or died. They also do not reflect resistance levels in the wider community. Even so, the direction they point in is clear, and ICMR itself has called for better antibiotic use, stronger infection control in hospitals and treatment guided by local resistance patterns.Asked what single change she would make, Dr Muralikumaran does not hesitate."We should start prescribing antibiotics only after establishing a bacterial disease," she says, "and pharmacies should start giving antibiotics based on a prescription."It is a modest-sounding request. It asks doctors to wait for a diagnosis, patients to finish the course they are given, and chemists to ask for the slip of paper. Each of those habits is small, and the damage from skipping them adds up across the country.
Article Summary: Antimicrobial resistance occurs when bacteria develop the ability to survive medicines that once killed them. An infection that a common antibiotic could treat becomes harder to control, pushing doctors toward stronger, costlier drugs. The report is clear that these are laboratory findings, and the right drug still has to be found.

NEW DELHI: Former England football captain David Beckham , a Unicef goodwill ambassador, has praised Heema Ninama from Madhya Pradesh's Jhabua district for standing up against child marriage and fighting for her right to continue her education.Beckham shared Heema's story on social media on November 20, marking World Children's Day, and applauded her courage and determination."I am sharing the story of 17-year-old Hima from Madhya Pradesh, India, who bravely stopped her own child marriage with the help of her school teachers. Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday took a swipe at the opposition, saying some people were still reluctant to acknowledge that 50 crore people had been lifted out of poverty in India.Addressing BJP workers virtually at a post-Diwali 'Sneh Milan' programme, PM Modi said the achievement reflected the success of his government's policies and efforts.He said those who sacrificed their lives for India's independence would be happiest to see poverty declining in the country.“All those who sacrificed their lives for independence, all those who dedicated their lives to freedom, all those who spent their youth in jails for independence, wherever their souls may be, today they must be the happiest seeing this World Bank report, thinking, ‘finally, poverty is leaving my country’,” PM Modi said.“A thousand years of slavery had impoverished us; for the first time after a thousand years of slavery, 50 crore people are coming out of poverty. There can be no greater satisfaction in life than this, no greater achievement than this,” he added.The PM, however, said some people were hesitant to acknowledge the achievement as it had been made during the BJP's tenure.“I know many people still hesitate to say this aloud, because all of this happened during this period (BJP rule).They don’t like it. Whether they like it or not, we have the satisfaction that our efforts have borne fruit,” PM Modi said.Describing the development as the beginning of a new chapter in people's lives, he said future generations would witness India's “golden era”.“Our intention is true, our policy is right, our direction is right, and there is no shortcoming in our hard work,” he said.According to a World Bank report, India's extreme poverty rate fell from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023, with an estimated 496 million people lifted out of poverty.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi says those who sacrificed their lives for India's independence would be happiest to see poverty declining in the country. NEW DELHI: Aazad Samaj Party (Kanshi Ram) chief Chandra Shekhar Azad on Sunday said that the alliance between Samajwadi Party and Congress is "not serious" about defeating Bharatiya Janata Party in the upcoming assembly polls in Uttar Pradesh.In an interview with news agency PTI, Azad said he had repeatedly pushed for a broader opposition alliance to take on the BJP but the SP and Congress had shown little interest in joining hands."They were not serious in 2024 either, nor in 2017, nor in 2019. And they will not be serious because atrocities happen against the poor and weak people. What atrocities are these leaders suffering?" he asked.Referring to the 2017 and 2022 assembly elections, Azad said the opposition needed to unite to match the BJP's vote share and improve its chances of defeating the ruling party."We saw the 2017 and 2022 elections. We formally sent messages to their responsible leaders. Whenever this topic came up, we stated, even through the media, that we want to fight together to stop the BJP," he said."And when we felt that they did not want it, we decided that a separate alliance should be formed because the alliances formed before were not successful in stopping the BJP," he added.Asked whether the possibility of an alliance with the SP and Congress remained open, Azad said his alliance is willing to make any sacrifice to bring the parties together."Yes… We have told them that we are ready to make any sacrifice. Article Title: Presidential election today? Trump confuses India with Brazil, claims 125 million voted
Article Text:
Trump says "125 million Indians voted in presidential election today."

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

US President Donald Trump on Monday confused India with Brazil, claiming that 125 million people had voted in an Indian “presidential election”, while also questioning the integrity of the American voting system.In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote, “125 Million People voted today in the first round of India’s Presidential Election. The results came out shortly after the vote closed, on the same day!”He then compared the alleged election results with the US electoral process, writing, “In Detroit, Philadelphia, California, and numerous other US Cities and States, the results, with much smaller numbers, will often take weeks to Rig, I mean, calculate. Voting in America is corrupt!!!”However, India did not hold a presidential election on Sunday. The President of India is elected indirectly by an electoral college and not through a direct nationwide popular vote.Trump's remarks came after Brazil held the first round of its presidential election on Sunday, with incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro advancing to the October 25 runoff.With 99.99% of the votes counted, Bolsonaro secured 47.03% of the valid votes, while Lula received 45.16%, according to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court.The figure of around 125 million mentioned by Trump is close to Brazil's total valid votes, which stood at about 125.27 million, suggesting he may have confused the Brazilian election with India.Neither Bolsonaro nor Lula crossed the 50% threshold required to win in the first round, triggering the October 25 runoff, BBC reported.Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, outperformed expectations in the first round and finished ahead of Lula. His strong showing has raised the prospect of a shift to the right in Latin America's largest economy.Brazil has used electronic voting for decades, and electoral authorities said the first-round voting process proceeded smoothly.The Organization of American States' electoral observation mission said “the voting has been going smoothly and under adequate safety conditions.”The rapid announcement of results has also been cited as a strength of Brazil's electronic voting system.“When results take a lot of time, it creates an opening for people to cast doubt on the results, to say there’s been a problem,” Josemar Lauriano Pereira, a 46-year-old lawyer in Rio de Janeiro, told the Associated Press.Trump's post drew reactions on social media, with users pointing out that India does not elect its president through a direct popular vote.One user posted, “Trump living in a different world? Is a presidential election taking place in India? President Donald Trump made the incorrect claim that 125 million people voted in India's "presidential election" today.”Another said, “What is my blud Donald Trump smoking? Why is he mentioning India instead of Brazil when talking about the election?”
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump confused India with Brazil, claiming that 125 million people had voted in an Indian "presidential election" He also questioned the integrity of the American voting system. India did not hold a presidential election on Sunday. The President of India is elected indirectly by an electoral college.

Article Title: “I can’t worry about my personal feelings”: Jerry Jones keeps Christian Parker’s Dallas Cowboys comeback alive after Mike Pettine’s defensive changes deliver a stunning win over Titans
Article Text:

Jerry Jones hints at Christian Parker's return to Cowboys playcalling

Christian Parker puts Cowboys ahead of personal feelings after demotion

Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones has left the door open for Christian Parker to reclaim his defensive playcalling duties. Mike Pettine took charge against the Tennessee Titans in Week 11 and helped Dallas secure a 51-30 victory. However, Jones does not seem ready to move on from Parker. His latest comments suggest the young defensive coordinator could still get another opportunity in Dallas.The Dallas Cowboys made the coaching change after six losses in their first 10 games of the 2026 season. They took playcalling duties away from Parker and handed them to senior defensive assistant Mike Pettine. The move produced encouraging results against Tennessee, but Jones made it clear that Parker remains part of his plans.During the postgame show on 105.3 The Fan, Cowboys insider Bobby Belt shared Jones' response when reporters asked about Parker's future.“Christian Parker, I’d say it’s more a fact that he’ll be calling plays again in the NFL and maybe with the Dallas Cowboys,” Jones said, according to Belt.That comment is significant because Parker has not lost his defensive coordinator position. Pettine has simply taken over the playcalling responsibilities, while Parker continues to work with the defensive unit.Pettine also had a strong first outing. The Cowboys kept the Titans out of the end zone in the first half, allowed only three points during that period and recorded five sacks against quarterback Cam Ward.However, Tennessee still finished with 30 points. Dallas also extended its unwanted streak of allowing at least 20 points in 18 consecutive games.Jones also discussed Parker's reaction during his appearance on 105.3 The Fan's K&C Masterpiece following the Week 11 victory.“I don’t have an issue, and I don’t think anybody else should if they know what I know,” Jones said.Parker had already addressed the situation during a press conference before the Titans game. Although he admitted that losing playcalling duties was difficult, he made it clear that he would not allow personal disappointment to affect the team.“It’s not an ideal situation for me personally, but it’s what’s best for the team at this current point,” Parker said.“I can’t worry about my personal feelings. I can’t worry about any of that. I’ve got to worry about the players. I’ve got to worry about the staff, to make sure that we handle business appropriately on Sunday. This isn’t gonna be a distraction.”His response appears to have impressed Jones, who believes Parker still has room to grow as a coach.Currently, Pettine will continue calling defensive plays as Dallas prepares for its Thanksgiving matchup against the Philadelphia Eagles on November 26. But Jones' comments offer Parker something valuable: the possibility of getting his old responsibilities back.The Cowboys now face an important stretch of their season, and their defensive performance will remain under scrutiny. If Pettine can maintain the improvement, Jones may have little reason to rush another change. However, Parker's experience and Jones' public backing mean his role in Dallas is far from settled. The coming weeks could offer a better picture of whether he gets another chance to call the defense.
Article Summary: Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones has left the door open for Christian Parker to reclaim his defensive playcalling duties. Mike Pettine took charge against the Tennessee Titans in Week 11 and helped Dallas secure a 51-30 victory. Jones made it clear that Parker remains part of his plans.

What Lies Ahead for Emmett Johnson? His Potential Role in the Chiefs' Offense

Emmett Johnson made the most of his big break when the Kansas City Chiefs gave him his first NFL start against the Atlanta Falcons. After an injury opened up a spot, he stepped up and played a great game. He proved he can both run the ball and catch passes, which gave the Chiefs another dependable playmaker. Scoring two touchdowns was a huge early milestone in his pro career, and it quickly won him praise from his teammates and coaches.Johnson earned his reputation as a star back during his time at Nebraska. Both scores came through the air, showing that Johnson could offer more than just a running option in the Chiefs' offense.Johnson finished the game with 101 rushing yards on 22 carries and six receptions for 70 yards. Reid also mentioned that Johnson has clearly earned the trust of his teammates. Those qualities helped him handle the responsibility of starting when the Chiefs needed him.Johnson's performance also caught the attention of Mahomes, who praised his ability to run hard, break tackles, and make plays as a receiver. Even though the Chiefs expected Kenneth Walker III back for their next game against the Arizona Cardinals, having both backs ready gives Andy Reid’s offense a nice boost, especially with Johnson's pass-catching skills and depth.For Johnson, the challenge will be to maintain the same preparation and consistency as the season progresses. Article Title: 30-year-old pitcher Tarik Skubal reportedly made the biggest deal of his career with a staggering $450 million for 9 years
Article Text:

How is Tarik Skubal's $450 million contract structured?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Mets get an ace, Dodgers step aside, lockout looms

Tarik Skubal has a new home and a new record. The two-time Cy Young Award winner agreed to a nine-year, $450 million contract with the New York Mets on Sunday, according to multiple sources. The deal has a full no-trade clause and no opt-outs. The club has not confirmed it because a physical is pending. At $50 million a year, the contract becomes the richest ever for a pitcher, surpassing Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal with the Dodgers. The Mets finished last in the NL East, and they went after the biggest arm on the market to fix it.Tarik Skubal gets a $45 million signing bonus, and it is shielded from the lockout that threatens the 2027 season (via AP). Another $30 million is deferred and will be paid from 2036 to 2045. The $50 million average tops the old pitcher high of $43.33 million, shared by Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander. Among all players, only Juan Soto ($765 million), Shohei Ohtani ($700 million) and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. ($500 million) have bigger totals.The $450 million left-hander turned 30 on Nov. 20. Over the past four seasons, he is 43-17 with a 2.42 ERA, striking out 655 batters and walking 95 in 546 innings.This year he went 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA in 26 starts for Detroit and Los Angeles, and he missed about six weeks after elbow surgery.Not everyone calls it a bargain. Los Angeles Times columnist Mirjam Swanson pointed to the length. "Skubal's is for the really long haul," she wrote, adding that he has had three elbow surgeries and will collect $50 million every season until he is 39.New York needed help. The Mets went 74-88 even with baseball's biggest opening-day payroll, about $352 million, and their starters posted a 4.47 ERA, 23rd in the majors. Skubal now leads a group that includes Nolan McLean, Christian Scott, Sean Manaea and Kodai Senga.Los Angeles never made an offer, ESPN's Alden Gonzalez reported. The Dodgers wanted him back and were willing to go long-term, but doubts over the new labor deal stopped them before a lockout. Skubal went 1-1 with a 2.45 ERA in two playoff starts for them before Milwaukee swept the NLCS.The signing lands about a week before owners are expected to lock out players. MLB has proposed a hard cap of $258.2 million for 2028, and Skubal and Soto alone would take nearly 40 per cent of it. One flag for the Mets is that his four-seam fastball averaged 96.8 mph this year, down from 97.6 in 2025.
Article Summary: Tarik Skubal agrees to nine-year, $450 million contract with New York Mets. At $50 million a year, the contract becomes the richest ever for a pitcher. Only Juan Soto, Shohei Ohtani and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. have bigger totals.

Alexander Zverev has been served with a fresh lawsuit from his former partner Brenda Patea over comments he made about their 2024 court case. The German tennis star received the legal papers on November 18 while competing at the ATP Finals in Turin. Patea, who shares a daughter with Zverev, claims he broke their private agreement by saying his innocence had been proven. Her lawyer wants the court to stop him from repeating those remarks and is also seeking financial damages.The new legal dispute comes from an interview Zverev gave to French sports newspaper L'Equipe after winning his first French Open title in June 2026. During the conversation, he was asked about the reaction from journalists who had covered his first Grand Slam victory despite the earlier allegations against him.Zverev did not appear pleased with the question. He responded by saying that the accusations had been proven false and asked the interviewer whether they knew that his innocence had been proven.However, Patea's lawyer Michael Scheele believes this was an incorrect account of what happened in court. He told the Daily Mail Sport that both sides had agreed not to discuss the case publicly after reaching an agreement in 2024.According to Scheele, Patea first tried to resolve the matter without taking further legal action. Her legal team sent letters asking Zverev not to repeat his comments. However, they received no response. Patea then filed a civil claim in Berlin on September 18.Scheele also explained why his client had initially taken a careful approach. Patea did not want to create further problems because she and Zverev share a daughter. She also depends on the financial support he provides for their child.The lawyer said Patea was upset after reading Zverev's comments in the media. He believes the remarks led to more criticism of his client and affected her public image and work as an influencer.Patea is now seeking an order that would prevent Zverev from making similar statements again. Her legal team has also asked for a penalty of up to €250,000 each time he breaks the proposed order.The latest lawsuit is connected to allegations Patea made against Zverev over an incident in May 2020. She accused him of pushing her against a wall and choking her during an argument in Berlin. Zverev has repeatedly denied the allegations.The case reached court in Germany in 2024. However, the proceedings ended after both sides agreed to a settlement. Zverev agreed to pay €150,000 to the state and €50,000 to a charity.Importantly, the court did not find him guilty or declare him innocent. The case was closed without a verdict, and the settlement did not amount to an admission of guilt.Patea's lawyer has also said that his client did not receive any personal compensation from Zverev as part of that agreement. He believes the public claim that Zverev's innocence was proven has added to the criticism she has faced.Meanwhile, Zverev's legal team has made its position clear. His lawyers, Christian Schertz and Anna Sophie Heuchemer, confirmed that they had received the lawsuit on November 18. They said their client would defend himself against the claims.The lawyers also argued that if Zverev made the comments as reported, they could be considered a protected expression of opinion under the German Constitution. They denied that he had broken any contractual agreement.Zverev has not personally commented on the new lawsuit. The legal dispute is now separate from the criminal case that ended in 2024, and the court has yet to decide on Patea's latest claims.

He stole vehicles, sold them for cash, broke into a Fleeca bank vault and targeted more businesses.Eventually, his earnings crossed $44,000. Article Title: India, Malaysia begin Harimau Shakti military drill with focus on counter-terror ops
Article Text:
Indian Army contingent in Malaysia for Exercise Hiramau Shakti. (Image credit: Indian Army)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The sixth edition of the India-Malaysia joint military exercise Harimau Shakti began on Friday at Ipoh in Malaysia, with 120 personnel from each side taking part. The exercise, a bilateral training event held alternately in the two countries, will run till November 30.The stated aim is to rehearse sub-conventional operations under Chapter VII of the United Nations mandate, with particular emphasis on synergising responses during counter-terrorism missions. The two armies will work in jungle and semi-urban terrain, relying on joint planning, tactical coordination and emerging technologies to improve interoperability.The exercise will unfold in phases. In the first phase, troops will first undergo cross-training to familiarise themselves with each other's operating procedures, followed by joint tactical drills. These include setting up a Joint Command Post and Surveillance Centre, counter-terrorism operations, raids, cordon-and-search drills and combat engineering tasks. Special attention will go to Unmanned Aerial Systems for reconnaissance and surveillance, along with counter-drone capabilities to detect and neutralise hostile unmanned platforms. The exercise will end with a validation drill built around a simulated counter-terrorism scenario, combining ground operations, integrated surveillance and unmanned systems.The fifth edition was held last year at the Mahajan Field Firing Range in Rajasthan from December 5 to 18 last year. The Indian contingent then largely comprised troops from the Dogra Regiment, while Malaysia was represented by the 25th Battalion of the Royal Malaysian Army.The exercise reflects a wider deepening of defence ties. India and Malaysia established diplomatic relations in 1957 and a Memorandum of Understanding on Defence Cooperation signed in 1993 gave military engagement an institutional framework. The Joint Defence Cooperation Committee reviews existing cooperation and identifies new areas. In August 2024, the two countries elevated their ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.The naval dimension has grown as well. The fourth edition of Samudra Laksamana was held at Lumut from September 9 to 12 this year, with INS Mysore exercising alongside the Royal Malaysian Navy's KD Lekir and KD Gagah Samudera.In October 2025 INS Sahyadri visited Kemaman, while the survey vessel INS Sandhayak made a port call at Klang in July 2025. The navies of both nations also take part in multilateral platforms such as MILAN and the ASEAN-India Maritime Exercise.Defence manufacturing is emerging as another area of cooperation. India is looking to expand exports to Southeast Asia, while Malaysia seeks to modernise its forces and diversify its sources of procurement. Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, Bharat Dynamics Limited and BEML showcased their products at LIMA 2025. The two countries are also co-chairing the SEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting-Plus (ADMM) counter-terrorism working group for 2024-2027.
Article Summary: The sixth edition of the India-Malaysia joint military exercise Harimau Shakti began on Friday at Ipoh in Malaysia. The exercise, a bilateral training event held alternately in the two countries, will run till November 30. The stated aim is to rehearse sub-conventional operations under Chapter VII of the United Nations mandate.

Article Title: Draymond Green gets dragged into explosive NBA legacy debate after Suns legend's brutal social media response
Article Text:
Draymond Green. Image via: Eakin Howard/Getty Images

What started the Draymond Green and Eddie Johnson argument?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Green questions Johnson's role, Johnson answers with numbers

Draymond Green and Eddie Johnson spent Sunday trading jabs on X over Green's Hall of Fame case. The former Suns Sixth Man of the Year started it after Warriors coach Steve Kerr said Stephen Curry's absence limits Green's offense. Johnson then asked if basketball is only a job for Green when Curry plays. The four-time champion fired back at Johnson's career and his analyst work. Johnson answered with a long list of his own numbers. Golden State has lost five straight games without Curry, which gave the argument extra bite.Kerr lit the fuse Saturday. "When Steph goes out, it really limits Draymond's impact offensively," the coach said. Johnson then posted on X (@Jumpshot8):"Name me a potential Hall of Fame player that will have that statistical personal résumé going into the Hall. Then you have players like Mark Aguirre, Tom Chambers, Shawn Marion, and Kevin Johnson not get in?"Green (@Money23Green) brushed it off: "Hahaha you named a bunch of players not named Eddie. Making it me vs. them is not changing your life, Ed."Johnson replied about 30 minutes later."My life is good, Draymond. Thanks for checking. I named Aguirre, Chambers, Marion and KJ for a reason. Your defense and impact on winning are part of your case. So here's the individual basketball question."He added his point with a question."How do you weigh that against the individual résumés of those four guys who could actually carry a team if the star player they played with is injured?"The last lines carried the sting. "Check my resume, even I did that many times. I got more players for you if you want? Just doing my job bro as an analyst. Isn't that your main job now and basketball is only when Curry plays?"Green's next post went after Johnson's role. Coming off the bench was "a great ROLE," he wrote, and he noted Johnson retired as the top scorer never to make an All-Star team.Johnson had numbers ready. He was a key piece on four conference finals teams, averaged about 22 points in 28 minutes during his Sixth Man of the Year season, scored over 20,000 points counting the playoffs and played in 94% of his teams' games across 17 seasons. "You said 'role' like it was an insult. Of all people, I figured you'd know better."He also plugged his podcast, Edification with Eddie Johnson. Green seized on it. "He's promoting his podcast!" he wrote, and added, "I'm happy to carry your show, though."Green scored nine points in the first quarter against Boston hours later, a season high.

Austin Reaves will miss his fifth straight game when the Lakers host the Utah Jazz on Monday. The one loss was a 109-97 defeat to Utah on Wednesday, which ended a nine-game winning streak.Redick laid it out with one stat. Through the first 12 games, Los Angeles had the league's top half-court offense, and Reaves was on the floor for 70% of those possessions. Over the last seven games, the half-court offense has been poor, and Reaves was on the court for 9%.Luka Doncic has felt it most. Sandro Mamukelashvili and Jake LaRavia have also cooled from three.Utah will be thin up front on Monday, with Lauri Markkanen and Jusuf Nurkic among those out. Article Title: Stephen Curry nearly falls out of his chair after Draymond Green pulls off something unforgettable against Celtics
Article Text:
Draymond Green and Stephen Curry. Image via: Getty Images

Why did Stephen Curry fall off his chair during Draymond Green's hot start?

Green's feud with Eddie Johnson and the Warriors' injury update

Stephen Curry could not stay seated on Sunday. The two-time MVP is out with a right oblique injury, but he was watching the Golden State Warriors host the Boston Celtics when Draymond Green hit his third 3-pointer of the first quarter, about six minutes in. Curry fell off his chair celebrating. Green has never been known as a scorer, so the burst surprised a lot of people. He had nine points, three rebounds and two assists at halftime, and Golden State led 44-42. The Warriors had entered the night on a five-game losing streak.Stephen Curry has been rehabbing since he got hurt against the Houston Rockets nearly two weeks ago, so Sunday gave him a rare reason to laugh. Draymond Green drilled three triples in the opening quarter, and the video of Curry tipping out of his seat is what fans latched onto. Steve Kerr said after Saturday's practice that Curry is back with the team and "in good spirits."Fans noticed right away. "even steph couldnt stay seated lol," @lily_irl887 posted. @trust_me_bro0 offered a different theory: "Steph just casually stretching. Nothing to do with Dray." Not every reply was a celebration. "Hasn't scored since," @dgant_3 wrote.The shooting was the real surprise. Green is an undersized center who has built his career on defense, and the Warriors needed the lift.Golden State failed to reach 100 points against the Spurs, Pelicans, Mavericks and Grizzlies in its last four losses, which came by an average of 27.3 points.Green is currently feuding with Suns legend Eddie Johnson, and he seemed to arrive with a point to make about his offense. Johnson reacted to Kerr's comments on Green's impact when Curry is off the floor, then questioned Green's Hall of Fame case by citing individual numbers.Green answered on his podcast and noted that Johnson scored 19,202 career points without a championship ring.Green was the defensive anchor on four title teams and six Finals teams, and his offensive peak likely came in Game 7 of the 2016 Finals, when he had 32 points, 15 rebounds and nine assists.One fan tied the two stories together. "He's feeling himself cause Eddie said he needs Steph 💀," @JOgetsbusy wrote.The Warriors went 0-5 on their recent road trip, and Curry missed the last four of those games. He was hurt against Houston and was first ruled out for two weeks, though the feeling around the team and league is the absence will run longer. The Warriors plan to share an injury update on Thanksgiving.

Article Title: 'Address: Tihar Jail, work: To Kill': How D-Company-linked gangster Naseem Durrani's long run ended in UP
Article Text:
Image Credit: TOI/ Special arrangement

How the net closed in

A chequered history





NEW DELHI: For years, Naseem Durrani moved between the gritty turf wars of northeast Delhi and the far-reaching shadow of Mumbai’s underworld — a man whose criminal ledger stretched from neighborhood extortion rackets to alleged hit contracts tied to Dawood Ibrahim ’s "D-Company."Beyond his crimes on the ground, Naseem actively used social media to cultivate a climate of fear among people. His Instagram profile served as an overt display of intimidation, featuring a bio that read: "Name: Badnaam (Notorious) | Address: Tihar Jail | Age: To live | Work: To kill." Through this digital persona, he openly advertised his criminal background while remaining absconding from law enforcement.On Friday, that long run ended in a hail of gunfire in Uttar Pradesh’s Bulandshahr district, where a joint operation by the Noida Special Task Force (STF) and Delhi Police cornered and killed the wanted gangster.Acting on intelligence inputs tracking Durrani’s movements, Delhi crime branch team led by DCP Sanjeev Yadav and deputy superintendent of police R K Mishra from STF Noida mounted a coordinated operation in Bulandshahr, supervised by special CP HGS Dhaliwal.In the early hours, the cops detected his movement near the Sikandra Bypass. CCTV footage showed him riding a scooter, and when the police team moved in to arrest him, he repeatedly looked back at the pursuing officers while speeding away.​During the chase, Naseem's scooter skidded and fell. Armed with two .32-bore pistols, he opened fire on the police team, prompting officers to retaliate. He sustained multiple gunshot wounds in the exchange of fire, and police recovered both pistols from the spot.The breakthrough came days after a brazen daylight-style shooting in northeast Delhi put law enforcement on high alert. Investigators had been scanning CCTV footage, tracing escape routes, and following leads in the wake of a deadly attack in Khajuri Khas.While police files linked Durrani to more than 25 criminal cases — spanning murder, attempt to murder, and robbery — his profile extended well beyond local street crime. The first was a killing outside Delhi law minister Kapil Mishra's camp office where 26-year-old Sameer was shot dead with over a dozen rounds fired in the attack.Police scrutiny following the recent violence has pointed to a prolonged gang feud in northeast Delhi, allegedly driven by extortion demands targeting shared auto-rickshaw operators and scrap dealers. Durrani had also previously been named as a key accused in the May 26 killing of Raja Mewati, alias "Akki Don," in Khajuri Khas.Investigators noted that Durrani had links to Dawood Ibrahim’s D-Company and remained in contact with underworld figure Chhota Shakeel. According to reports, Shakeel had allegedly handed Durrani a contract during 2016–2017 to eliminate rival gangster Chhota Rajan, who was lodged in Tihar Jail.With Durrani killed in the Bulandshahr encounter, investigators are expected to examine how his network operated across the Delhi-NCR and western Uttar Pradesh belt, as well as any lingering fallout from the ongoing turf wars in northeast Delhi.
Article Summary: Gangster Naseem Durrani was shot dead by police in Bulandshahr, Uttar Pradesh. He was wanted in more than 25 criminal cases spanning murder, attempt to murder, and robbery. His criminal ledger stretched from neighborhood extortion rackets to alleged hit contracts tied to Dawood Ibrahim’s "D-Company"

Article Title: Meta AI head Alexandr Wang warns about AI; says: Superintelligence is coming, but how 'dangerous' it will be depends on humans as ...
Article Text:
Alexandr Wang: ’Superintelligence is coming’

AI moving beyond human expertise

What he expects next

A call for a different path

Read Alexandr Wang’s complete post here

Superintelligence is arriving. How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in. As someone who has spent much of my life in math and science, I see the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as clearly marking the beginning of a significant change.

For most who have studied math, this represents the absolute pinnacle of intellectual accomplishment—nothing humanity has ever accomplished compares to proving the Riemann Hypothesis in terms of sheer intellectual might and strength.

As someone who grew up in Los Alamos, New Mexico, many physicists would agree that the discovery of the atomic bomb is a homework problem compared to the Riemann Hypothesis. It is hard to overstate the magnitude of discovery that we have just witnessed—completed with the help of an alien mind that we don’t understand.

For those who did math competitions, there was a similar moment of “oh shit everything is about to change” when the models began acing the AIME in December 2024 with o3. The hardest AIME problems are much harder in terms of sheer intellectual difficulty than the problems that even the most advanced engineers and business people need to solve on a day-to-day basis. There of course is domain-specific knowledge, context, know-how, and other tactical constraints that were needed to unlock the models across other areas, but lack of raw intelligence was not the bottleneck.

And in fact, the progress across other domains over the past 2 years as we’ve mitigated these non-intelligence factors has been immense—we have seen coding be nearly solved, the emergence of extremely powerful cyber capabilities, and strong agentic capabilities which have enabled the models to become general-purpose useful aides.

Again the key insight here was simply that the hardest AIME problems are intellectually very difficult, far more difficult than most coding work, most cyber work, most business work, etc.,

and over the past two years we have been filling in the gaps to enable the models to accomplish those things.

To be clear, AIME is an extracurricular activity for teenagers; the Riemann Hypothesis may be the most intellectually demanding problem humanity has ever devised, which some of the most brilliant humans over the past 150 years have dedicated their lives to. At MIT, my professors would have said the hardest intellectual problems in nearly every major field of human study are “easier” than the Riemann Hypothesis, albeit with other challenges such as experimentation, data, and feedback loops.

The remaining gaps for models to greatly surpass humanity in every field are no longer intelligence; they are domain-specific know-how, plumbing, and experimentation. This means it is likely that AI will become the greatest contributor of progress across nearly every field, vastly outperforming the best humans.

Notably, this is likely true of AI research. Most researchers would agree that AI research is certainly much less intellectually demanding than solving the Riemann Hypothesis.

The models are clearly going to be intelligent enough to automate all of AI research and be clearly superhuman at improving themselves—along with massively accelerating biological research, weapons research, economics research, and more.

The implications are enormous. In the same way that the math community has not fully digested the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, nearly every field could be accelerated at a pace beyond what humans can understand or monitor.

It is now incredibly important for us to be thoughtful about the future we want and how we get there. It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement. It is equally hard to imagine a world where humanity maintains control with superintelligence that is 1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field. Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

I notice a particular form of lazy thinking within the AI industry, which is that ASI is inevitable and the only problem to solve is how to do it safely, but there is much more at stake. We should not be okay with a “handover” of society to AI. We should endeavor ourselves to build a technology which delivers a positive future for humanity, where all humans have greater agency and empowerment. I strongly believe this is possible, but likely involves the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the “default path” in front of us.

Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang has issued a serious warning about the rapid growth of artificial intelligence, saying that the world may already be entering the era of superintelligence. In a lengthy post shared on social media platform X (formerly known As Twitter) Wang said that next year could prove critical in determining whether increasingly powerful AI systems benefit humanity or lead to outcomes that are difficult for humans to control. The comments made by Wang come amid the growing debate within technology industry over the pace of the development of AI. He also acknowledged the potential of AI in accelerating scientific and economic progress. He further emphasised that humanity must remain actively involved in shaping its future rather than enabling the society to be handed over to machines.In his post, Wang declared that "superintelligence is arriving" and argued that recent AI breakthroughs suggest machines are rapidly approaching, and in some areas surpassing, the highest levels of human intellectual performance. He pointed to the reported proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems, as a milestone that demonstrates the scale of change underway.Wang described the achievement as an intellectual accomplishment unlike anything humanity has seen before and said it showcased the capabilities of what he referred to as an "alien mind" that humans do not fully understand.According to Wang, the development marks a turning point similar to the moment AI models began solving highly difficult American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME) problems, signalling that raw intelligence was no longer the primary limitation for advanced AI systems.Wang argued that many of the toughest mathematical challenges are more intellectually demanding than most real-world tasks performed by engineers, cybersecurity experts or business professionals. He feels that the as the capabilities of AI have improved, the practical limitations have been reduced and the AI models have also become quite effective across coding, cybersecurity and other sectors. He also emphasised that the remaining obstacles for AI systems are mainly related to the domain knowledge, experimentation and implementation rather than intelligence itself. Wang feels that as a result, AI is expected to become a main contributor to growth across almost every field of human activity."The remaining gaps for models to greatly surpass humanity in every field are no longer intelligence," he wrote, suggesting that future systems could significantly outperform the best human experts in many disciplines.Wang said the remaining obstacles to AI surpassing humans in every field are domain know-how, infrastructure and experimentation, not intelligence. He concluded that AI will likely become the largest contributor to progress in nearly every field, outperforming the best humans. That includes AI research itself, which he called less demanding than the Riemann Hypothesis. Models, he said, will be smart enough to automate all of it and to improve themselves in a clearly superhuman way, while speeding up biological, weapons and economics research. He warned that fields could advance faster than humans can understand or monitor.Wang said it is hard to imagine humanity keeping control over unconstrained recursive self-improvement, or over a superintelligence 1,000 times smarter than people in every field. He argued the scientific and technical problems of capability progress are likely solved, so the urgent work is safety, alignment and security, along with deciding how progress should unfold. He criticized what he called lazy thinking in the AI industry: the idea that superintelligence is inevitable and only doing it safely remains. Society should not accept handing itself over to AI, he said, and should aim for technology that gives all humans greater agency. That likely requires the whole industry to depart from the default path, he added.
Article Summary: Alexandr Wang: How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in. Wang: The proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is clearly marking the beginning of a significant change. He says AI will become the greatest contributor of progress across nearly every field, vastly outperforming the best humans.
